title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: The Different Ways of Employing Capital

Every form of capital is meant to support productive labour, and nothing else. Even so, the amount of labour that equal capitals can set in motion varies enormously depending on how each one is used. The value that this employment adds to a country's annual output of land and labour varies just as much.

There are four ways to employ capital. First, you can use it to obtain the raw produce that society needs each year for its own use and consumption. Second, you can use it to manufacture and prepare that raw produce so it is ready for immediate use. Third, you can use it to transport either the raw or the manufactured produce from places where it is plentiful to places where it is wanted. Fourth, you can use it to break particular portions of either kind into parcels small enough to suit the occasional needs of buyers. The first way describes the capital of everyone who undertakes the improvement or cultivation of land, mines, or fisheries. The second describes the capital of every master manufacturer. The third describes the capital of every wholesale merchant. The fourth describes the capital of every retailer. It is hard to imagine any use of capital that does not fall under one of these four headings.
Each of these four methods is absolutely necessary, either to the existence or growth of the other three, or to the general convenience of society.
Unless some capital were used to supply raw produce in reasonable abundance, no manufactures and no trade of any kind could exist at all.

Unless some capital were used to manufacture the part of the raw produce that needs a good deal of preparation before it is fit for use, that produce would either never be made, because there would be no demand for it, or, if it grew on its own, it would have no exchange value and would add nothing to society's wealth.

Unless some capital were used to carry the raw or manufactured produce from places where it is plentiful to places where it is wanted, no more of either would be produced than the neighbourhood itself could consume. The merchant's capital exchanges the surplus produce of one place for that of another, and in doing so it stimulates the industry and increases the enjoyments of both.

Unless some capital were used to break and divide portions of the raw or manufactured produce into parcels small enough to suit occasional buyers, everyone would have to buy a larger quantity of any good than his immediate needs required. Suppose, for example, there were no such trade as a butcher's. Then everyone would have to buy a whole ox or a whole sheep at a time. That would generally be inconvenient for the rich and far more so for the poor. If a poor workman had to buy a month's or six months' provisions at once, he would be forced to shift a large part of the stock he uses as capital, his tools or his shop's furnishings, the part that earns him an income, into the part of his stock reserved for immediate consumption, which earns him nothing. Nothing could be more convenient for such a person than to be able to buy his food day by day, or even hour by hour, as he needs it. That lets him keep almost his whole stock working as capital. It lets him produce work of greater value, and the profit he earns this way far more than makes up for the extra price that the retailer's profit adds to the goods. The prejudice some political writers hold against shopkeepers and tradesmen has no foundation. There is no need to tax them or limit their numbers; on the contrary, they can never become so numerous as to harm the public, though they may become numerous enough to harm one another. The quantity of grocery goods that can be sold in a given town, for example, is limited by the demand of that town and its surroundings. So the capital that can be used in the grocery trade there cannot exceed what is needed to buy that quantity. If this capital is split between two grocers, their competition tends to make both sell cheaper than a single grocer would. If it is split among twenty, the competition is that much fiercer, and the chance of their conspiring to raise the price is that much smaller. Their competition might perhaps ruin some of them, but that is their own affair, and it can safely be left to their judgment. It can never harm either the consumer or the producer; on the contrary, it must make retailers both sell cheaper and buy dearer than they would if one or two people monopolised the whole trade. Some of them may now and then lure a weak customer into buying what he does not need. But this harm is too trivial to deserve public attention, and limiting their numbers would not necessarily prevent it anyway. To take the most suspect example, it is not the multitude of alehouses that produces a general tendency toward drunkenness among ordinary people; rather, that tendency, which springs from other causes, inevitably keeps a multitude of alehouses in business.

The people whose capitals are employed in any of these four ways are themselves productive labourers. Their labour, when it is well directed, fixes and embodies itself in the saleable commodity it works on, and it generally adds to that commodity's price at least the value of their own maintenance and consumption. The profits of the farmer, the manufacturer, the merchant, and the retailer are all drawn from the price of the goods, which the first two produce and the last two buy and sell. Yet equal capitals employed in these four different ways will set in motion very different quantities of productive labour, and they will increase the value of society's annual output of land and labour in very different proportions.

The retailer's capital replaces the capital of the merchant from whom he buys his goods, together with its profits, and so enables that merchant to carry on his business. The retailer himself is the only productive labourer his capital directly employs. The whole value that his employment adds to society's annual output consists of his profit.

The wholesale merchant's capital replaces the capitals of the farmers and manufacturers from whom he buys the raw and manufactured produce he deals in, together with their profits, and so enables them to carry on their respective trades. This is the main way he indirectly helps to support society's productive labour and to increase the value of its annual output. His capital also employs the sailors and carriers who move his goods from place to place, and it raises the price of those goods by the value not only of his profits but of their wages too. That is all the productive labour his capital directly sets in motion and all the value it directly adds to the annual output. On both counts its effect is considerably greater than that of the retailer's capital.

Part of the master manufacturer's capital is fixed capital tied up in the tools of his trade, and it replaces, together with its profits, the capital of some other craftsman from whom he buys them. Part of his circulating capital goes to buy materials, and it replaces, with their profits, the capitals of the farmers and miners from whom he buys them. But a large part of it is always distributed, either yearly or over much shorter periods, among the various workmen he employs. It raises the value of those materials by the workmen's wages and by the masters' profits on the whole stock of wages, materials, and tools used in the business. So it directly sets in motion a much greater quantity of productive labour, and adds far more value to society's annual output of land and labour, than an equal capital in the hands of any wholesale merchant.

No equal capital sets in motion more productive labour than the farmer's. Not only his labouring servants but his labouring cattle are productive labourers. In agriculture, moreover, Nature works alongside man; and though her labour costs nothing, its produce has value just as the most expensive workman's does. The most important operations of farming seem designed not so much to increase Nature's fertility, though they do that too, as to direct it toward the plants most useful to man. A field overgrown with briars and brambles may often yield as much vegetable matter as the best-tended vineyard or cornfield. Planting and tilling often regulate Nature's active fertility more than they stir it up, and after all this labour a great part of the work is still left for her to do. The labourers and labouring cattle used in agriculture therefore do not merely reproduce a value equal to their own consumption, or to the capital that employs them together with its owner's profits, as workmen in manufactures do; they reproduce a much greater value. Beyond the farmer's capital and all its profits, they regularly reproduce the landlord's rent as well. This rent may be regarded as the produce of those powers of Nature whose use the landlord lends to the farmer. It is larger or smaller depending on the supposed extent of those powers, or in other words on the supposed natural or improved fertility of the land. It is the work of Nature that remains after subtracting or paying for everything that can be counted as the work of man. It is seldom less than a quarter, and often more than a third, of the whole produce. No equal quantity of productive labour employed in manufactures can ever bring about so great a reproduction. In manufactures Nature does nothing; man does everything; and the reproduction must always match the strength of the agents that cause it. So capital employed in agriculture not only sets in motion more productive labour than any equal capital employed in manufactures; in proportion to the productive labour it employs, it also adds far more value to the country's annual output of land and labour, and to the real wealth and revenue of its people. Of all the ways capital can be employed, this is by far the most beneficial to society.

The capitals employed in a society's agriculture and retail trade must always stay within that society. Their use is confined almost to an exact spot, the farm or the retailer's shop. And as a rule, though there are exceptions, they belong to resident members of the society.
The wholesale merchant's capital, by contrast, seems to have no fixed or necessary home anywhere. It can wander from place to place, going wherever it can buy cheap or sell dear.

The manufacturer's capital must, of course, sit wherever the manufacturing is done; but where that will be is not always fixed. It may often be a great distance both from where the materials grow and from where the finished product is consumed. Lyons lies far from both the places that supply the materials of its manufactures and the places that consume them. Fashionable people in Sicily dress in silks made in other countries from materials Sicily itself produces. Part of Spain's wool is manufactured in Great Britain, and some of that cloth is later shipped back to Spain.

Whether the merchant whose capital exports a society's surplus produce is a native or a foreigner matters very little. If he is a foreigner, the number of the society's productive labourers is smaller by just one man than it would be if he were a native, and the value of its annual output is smaller by that one man's profits. The sailors or carriers he employs may belong, just as they would if he were a native, either to his country, or to theirs, or to some third country. A foreigner's capital gives value to their surplus produce just as a native's would, by exchanging it for something there is demand for at home. It replaces the capital of the person who produced that surplus just as effectively, and enables him to carry on his business just as effectively, which is the very service by which a wholesale merchant's capital chiefly helps to support productive labour and to increase the value of his society's annual output.

It matters more that the manufacturer's capital should reside within the country. It necessarily sets in motion more productive labour and adds more value to society's annual output of land and labour. Still, such capital may be very useful to a country even if it does not reside there. The capitals of the British manufacturers who work up the flax and hemp imported each year from the Baltic coasts are surely very useful to the countries that produce them. Those materials are part of those countries' surplus produce, which, unless it were exchanged each year for something they want, would have no value and would soon stop being produced. The merchants who export it replace the capitals of the people who produce it, and so encourage them to keep producing; and the British manufacturers in turn replace the capitals of those merchants.

A particular country, like a particular person, may often lack the capital to do all three things at once: improve and cultivate all its land, manufacture and prepare its whole raw produce for immediate use, and carry the surplus, raw or manufactured, to those distant markets where it can be exchanged for something wanted at home. The people of many parts of Great Britain do not have enough capital to improve and cultivate all their land. Much of the wool of the southern counties of Scotland is manufactured in Yorkshire, after a long overland haul on very bad roads, for lack of capital to manufacture it at home. There are many small manufacturing towns in Great Britain whose inhabitants lack the capital to carry the produce of their own industry to the distant markets where there is demand for it. If there are any merchants among them, they are really only the agents of wealthier merchants who live in some of the great commercial cities.

When a country's capital is not enough for all three of these purposes, the larger the share of it that goes into agriculture, the greater the quantity of productive labour it sets in motion within the country, and the greater the value its employment adds to society's annual output of land and labour. After agriculture, capital employed in manufactures sets in motion the most productive labour and adds the most value to the annual output. Capital employed in the export trade has the least effect of the three.

A country that lacks enough capital for all three purposes has not yet reached the degree of wealth it seems naturally destined for. But to try, prematurely and with insufficient capital, to do all three at once is certainly not the quickest way for a society to acquire enough capital, any more than it would be for an individual. The combined capital of all a nation's individuals has its limits, just as a single person's does, and it can accomplish only so much. It grows the same way a single person's does: by continually accumulating and adding whatever people save out of their revenue. It is likely to grow fastest, then, when it is employed in the way that yields the greatest revenue to all the country's inhabitants, since that lets them save the most. And the revenue of all a country's inhabitants is necessarily proportional to the value of the annual output of their land and labour.

The main reason our American colonies have advanced so rapidly toward wealth and greatness is that almost all their capital has so far gone into agriculture. They have no manufactures except the household and coarser kinds that naturally accompany the progress of agriculture and that the women and children of every household make. Most of America's export and coasting trade is carried on by the capitals of merchants who live in Great Britain. Even the stores and warehouses from which goods are retailed in some provinces, especially Virginia and Maryland, belong in many cases to merchants who live in the mother country, and they form one of the few cases where a society's retail trade is run by the capital of non-resident people. If the Americans were, by combination or any other kind of force, to stop importing European manufactures and, by giving a monopoly to those of their own countrymen who could make the same goods, divert any large part of their capital into this employment, they would slow down rather than speed up the further growth in the value of their annual output, and would block rather than promote their country's progress toward real wealth and greatness. This would be even more true if they tried in the same way to monopolise their whole export trade.

Indeed, human prosperity has scarcely ever lasted long enough to let any great country accumulate capital sufficient for all three purposes, unless we credit the marvellous accounts of the wealth and cultivation of China, of ancient Egypt, and of ancient Hindustan. Even those three countries, the wealthiest by every account that ever existed, are chiefly famous for their superiority in agriculture and manufactures. They do not seem to have been distinguished for foreign trade. The ancient Egyptians had a superstitious dread of the sea; a similar superstition prevails among the Indians; and the Chinese have never excelled in foreign commerce. Most of the surplus produce of all three countries seems always to have been exported by foreigners, who gave in exchange something else for which they found a demand there, frequently gold and silver.

In this way, then, the same capital will set in motion a greater or smaller quantity of productive labour in a country, and add a greater or smaller value to its annual output of land and labour, depending on the different proportions in which it is employed in agriculture, manufactures, and wholesale trade. And the difference is very great even among the different kinds of wholesale trade in which part of it may be employed.

All wholesale trade, all buying in order to sell again wholesale, can be reduced to three kinds: the home trade, the foreign trade of consumption, and the carrying trade. The home trade buys in one part of a country and sells in another the produce of that country's industry. It covers both the inland and the coasting trade. The foreign trade of consumption buys foreign goods for home consumption. The carrying trade conducts the commerce of foreign countries, carrying the surplus produce of one to another.

Capital employed in buying in one part of the country to sell in another, dealing in the produce of that country's own industry, generally replaces, with each such operation, two separate capitals that had both been employed in that country's agriculture or manufactures, and so enables them to keep going. When it sends out a certain value of goods from the merchant's home base, it generally brings back at least an equal value of other goods. When both are the produce of domestic industry, each such operation necessarily replaces two separate capitals that had both been supporting productive labour, and so lets them go on supporting it. The capital that ships Scotch manufactures to London and brings back English corn and manufactures to Edinburgh necessarily replaces, with each such operation, two British capitals that had both been employed in the agriculture or manufactures of Great Britain.

Capital employed in buying foreign goods for home consumption, when the purchase is made with the produce of domestic industry, also replaces two separate capitals with each operation, but only one of them is employed in supporting domestic industry. The capital that ships British goods to Portugal and brings back Portuguese goods to Great Britain replaces, with each operation, only one British capital. The other is Portuguese. So even if the returns of the foreign trade of consumption came as quickly as those of the home trade, the capital employed in it would give only half as much encouragement to the country's industry and productive labour.

But the returns of the foreign trade of consumption are very rarely as quick as those of the home trade. The returns of the home trade generally come in before the year is out, and sometimes three or four times in a year. The returns of the foreign trade of consumption seldom come in before the year is out, and sometimes not for two or three years. So a capital employed in the home trade may complete twelve operations, being sent out and brought back twelve times, before a capital in the foreign trade of consumption completes one. If the two capitals are equal, then, the one will give twenty-four times more encouragement and support to the country's industry than the other.

Sometimes the foreign goods for home consumption are bought not with the produce of domestic industry but with some other foreign goods. But those other foreign goods must themselves have been bought, either directly with the produce of domestic industry or with something else that had been bought with it; for, except in cases of war and conquest, foreign goods can only ever be obtained in exchange for something produced at home, either directly or after two or more exchanges. So the effects of capital employed in this kind of roundabout foreign trade of consumption are in every way the same as those of capital in the most direct trade of the same kind, except that the final returns are likely to be even more distant, since they depend on the returns of two or three separate foreign trades. If the hemp and flax of Riga are bought with the tobacco of Virginia, which had been bought with British manufactures, the merchant must wait for the returns of two separate foreign trades before he can use the same capital to buy a like quantity of British manufactures again. If the Virginia tobacco had been bought not with British manufactures but with the sugar and rum of Jamaica, which had been bought with those manufactures, he must wait for the returns of three. If these two or three separate foreign trades happen to be run by two or three separate merchants, the second buying the goods imported by the first and the third buying those imported by the second in order to export them again, then each merchant does get the returns of his own capital more quickly; but the final returns of the whole capital employed in the trade are just as slow as ever. Whether the whole capital in such a roundabout trade belongs to one merchant or to three makes no difference to the country, though it may to the individual merchants. In both cases three times as much capital must be employed to exchange a given value of British manufactures for a given quantity of flax and hemp as would have been needed if the manufactures and the flax and hemp had been exchanged directly for one another. So the whole capital employed in such a roundabout foreign trade of consumption will generally give less encouragement and support to the country's productive labour than an equal capital in a more direct trade of the same kind.

Whatever the foreign commodity used to buy the foreign goods for home consumption, it can make no essential difference to the nature of the trade or to the encouragement it gives to the country's productive labour. If the goods are bought with the gold of Brazil, say, or the silver of Peru, that gold and silver, like the tobacco of Virginia, must have been bought with something that was either the produce of the country's industry or had itself been bought with something that was. So, as far as the country's productive labour is concerned, the foreign trade of consumption carried on by means of gold and silver has all the advantages and all the drawbacks of any other equally roundabout foreign trade of consumption, and it replaces the capital that directly supports productive labour just as fast, or just as slowly. It does seem to have one advantage over any other equally roundabout foreign trade. Because these metals are small in bulk and great in value, moving them from place to place is less expensive than moving almost any other foreign goods of equal worth. Their freight costs much less, their insurance is no greater, and no goods are less likely to be damaged in transit. So an equal quantity of foreign goods can often be bought with a smaller quantity of domestic produce by the use of gold and silver than by the use of any other foreign goods. In this way the country's demand can often be met more fully, and at a smaller cost, than in any other. Whether the continual export of these metals tends in any other way to impoverish the country that carries it on, I shall have occasion to examine at great length later.

The part of any country's capital that goes into the carrying trade is withdrawn entirely from supporting that country's own productive labour and put to supporting the productive labour of foreign countries instead. It may replace two separate capitals with each operation, but neither of them belongs to that country. The Dutch merchant's capital that carries the corn of Poland to Portugal and brings back the fruits and wines of Portugal to Poland replaces, with each such operation, two capitals, neither of which had been supporting the productive labour of Holland; one was supporting Poland's, the other Portugal's. Only the profits return regularly to Holland, and they make up the whole addition this trade necessarily makes to that country's annual output of land and labour. When a country does carry on its carrying trade with its own ships and sailors, the part of the capital that pays the freight is distributed among, and sets in motion, a certain number of that country's productive labourers. Almost every nation that has had a sizeable share of the carrying trade has in fact carried it on this way. The trade probably got its name from this, the people of such countries being the carriers for others. But it does not seem essential to the nature of the trade that this should be so. A Dutch merchant may, for example, employ his capital in handling the commerce of Poland and Portugal by carrying part of one country's surplus produce to the other, not in Dutch but in British ships. We may suppose he actually does so on some occasions. It is on this account that the carrying trade has been thought especially advantageous to a country like Great Britain, whose defence and security depend on the number of its sailors and ships. But the same capital can employ as many sailors and ships in the foreign trade of consumption, or even in the home trade when it is carried on by coasting vessels, as it could in the carrying trade. The number of sailors and ships any given capital can employ does not depend on the nature of the trade, but partly on the bulk of the goods in proportion to their value and partly on the distance between the ports they are carried between, chiefly on the former of these two. The coal trade from Newcastle to London, for instance, employs more shipping than all the carrying trade of England, though the ports are not far apart. So forcing, by extraordinary inducements, a larger share of a country's capital into the carrying trade than would naturally go there will not always increase that country's shipping.

The capital employed in a country's home trade, then, will generally encourage and support more productive labour in that country, and raise the value of its annual output more, than an equal capital employed in the foreign trade of consumption; and the capital in this latter trade has, on both counts, a still greater advantage over an equal capital in the carrying trade. The wealth of every country, and, so far as power depends on wealth, the power of every country, must always be proportional to the value of its annual output, the fund from which all taxes are ultimately paid. And the great aim of every country's political economy is to increase that country's wealth and power. It ought therefore to give no preference or special encouragement to the foreign trade of consumption over the home trade, nor to the carrying trade over either of the other two. It ought neither to force nor to entice a greater share of the country's capital into either of those channels than would naturally flow into them of its own accord.
Each of these branches of trade, however, is not only beneficial but necessary and unavoidable when the natural course of things introduces it without any constraint or force.

When the produce of any branch of industry exceeds what the country's demand requires, the surplus must be sent abroad and exchanged for something there is demand for at home. Without such exporting, part of the country's productive labour would have to stop, and the value of its annual output would fall. The land and labour of Great Britain generally produce more corn, woollens, and hardware than the home market demands. So the surplus of these must be sent abroad and exchanged for something wanted at home. Only through such exporting can this surplus gain enough value to repay the labour and expense of producing it. The seacoast and the banks of all navigable rivers are good locations for industry only because they make it easier to export this surplus and exchange it for something more in demand there.

When the foreign goods bought with the surplus produce of domestic industry exceed the demand of the home market, the surplus part of them must be sent abroad again and exchanged for something more in demand at home. About 96,000 hogsheads of tobacco are bought each year in Virginia and Maryland with part of the surplus produce of British industry. But Great Britain's demand probably requires no more than 14,000. So if the remaining 82,000 could not be sent abroad and exchanged for something more in demand at home, their importation would have to stop at once, and with it the productive labour of all those people in Great Britain now employed in preparing the goods used to buy these 82,000 hogsheads. Those goods, being part of the produce of Britain's land and labour, would have no market at home and would be cut off from the one they had abroad, so they would cease to be produced. The most roundabout foreign trade of consumption, then, may on some occasions be just as necessary for supporting the country's productive labour and the value of its annual output as the most direct.

When a country's capital stock grows so large that it cannot all be employed in supplying that country's consumption and supporting its productive labour, the surplus naturally spills over into the carrying trade and is used to perform the same services for other countries. The carrying trade is the natural effect and symptom of great national wealth, but it does not seem to be its natural cause. Statesmen inclined to give it special encouragement seem to have mistaken the effect and symptom for the cause. Holland, by far the richest country in Europe for the extent of its land and the number of its people, accordingly has the greatest share of Europe's carrying trade. England, perhaps the second richest country in Europe, is also supposed to have a considerable share in it, though much of what usually passes for England's carrying trade will often turn out to be no more than a roundabout foreign trade of consumption. That is largely true of the trades that carry the goods of the East and West Indies and of America to the various European markets. Those goods are generally bought either directly with the produce of British industry or with something else that had been bought with that produce, and the final returns of these trades are generally used or consumed in Great Britain. The trade carried on in British ships between the various Mediterranean ports, and some trade of the same kind carried on by British merchants between the various ports of India, make up, perhaps, the main branches of what is properly Great Britain's carrying trade.

The extent of the home trade, and of the capital that can be employed in it, is necessarily limited by the value of the surplus produce of all the distant places within the country that have occasion to exchange their products with one another. The extent of the foreign trade of consumption is limited by the value of the surplus produce of the whole country and of what can be bought with it. The extent of the carrying trade is limited by the value of the surplus produce of all the different countries in the world. Its possible scope, then, is in a sense infinite compared with that of the other two, and it is capable of absorbing the greatest capitals.

The thought of his own private profit is the only motive that decides the owner of any capital to put it into agriculture, manufactures, or some particular branch of wholesale or retail trade. The different quantities of productive labour it may set in motion, and the different values it may add to society's annual output of land and labour depending on how it is used, never cross his mind. So in countries where agriculture is the most profitable of all employments, and where farming and improvement are the most direct roads to a splendid fortune, individuals' capitals will naturally be put to the use most advantageous to the whole society. The profits of agriculture, however, seem to have no edge over those of other employments anywhere in Europe. To be sure, in every corner of it projectors have, in recent years, amused the public with the most magnificent accounts of the profits to be made by cultivating and improving land. Without going into the details of their calculations, a very simple observation may convince us the results must be false. We see every day the most splendid fortunes acquired in a single lifetime through trade and manufactures, often from a very small capital, sometimes from no capital at all. A single instance of such a fortune made by agriculture in the same time and from such a capital has perhaps not occurred in Europe during the present century. Yet in all the great countries of Europe much good land still lies uncultivated, and most of what is cultivated is far from improved to the degree it is capable of. Agriculture, then, is almost everywhere capable of absorbing much more capital than has ever yet been put into it. What features of European policy have given the trades carried on in towns so great an advantage over the one carried on in the country, that private people often find it more to their advantage to employ their capital in the most distant carrying trades of Asia and America than in improving and cultivating the most fertile fields in their own neighbourhood, I shall try to explain fully in the next two books.
